tour.title: Higashiyama & Gion: Temples, Lanes & Geisha Streets
tour.summary: A downhill half-day from the great temple on stilts to the river at dusk — preserved stone slopes, a widow's memorial to the man who unified Japan, a shrine that launched a 1,150-year festival, and the lanes where geiko still work.
tour.overviewText:
Kyoto in winter is a city with the volume turned down. The buses thin, the maples are bare, the temples stand in cold blue light with nobody in them — and then a plum tree opens, weeks before the cherries, and you remember that people have watched the seasons from here for twelve hundred years. Today you walk the eastern edge of the old capital: Higashiyama, "eastern mountains", the wooded ridge where Kyoto has always put its holiest buildings.

Kyoto was Japan's capital for more than a thousand years. Emperor Kanmu founded it in 794 as Heian-kyō, "capital of peace and tranquillity", on a Chinese plan borrowed from Chang'an, the Tang dynasty capital: a rectangle of numbered avenues with the palace at the top. The court stayed until 1868, when the Meiji government moved the emperor to Tokyo. Kyoto escaped the firebombing that destroyed most Japanese cities in the Second World War, which is why so much of what you stand in front of is original timber, not a rebuild.

Two faiths share this ground. Shinto, Japan's older religion, is a faith of places: shrines, called jinja, mark where a kami — a spirit or deity, of nature or legend — is felt to be present, and a torii gate marks the threshold. Buddhism arrived from the mainland in the sixth century with temples, called tera, plus graveyards and Kannon, the bodhisattva of compassion. Most Japanese families use both without contradiction: shrines for blessings in this life, temples for funerals and the dead. For a thousand years the two were tangled together, until 1868, when the Meiji government ordered them separated by law.

These streets encode an argument. Kyoto now lives largely on visitors, and Higashiyama is where the bill comes due. The lanes below Kiyomizu-dera were among Japan's first protected streetscapes, saved in the 1970s; today they carry more visitors in an afternoon than residents all week, and the people who fought to keep the machiya — the narrow wooden townhouses — now ask visitors to keep moving and keep quiet. In Gion the neighbours barred photography in the private lanes and posted fines.

The route is a descent, deliberately. Begin high on the hillside at Kiyomizu-dera, the temple on its wooden stage, and walk down through the preserved slopes and the memorial temple of Toyotomi Hideyoshi into the shrine at the heart of Gion. From there the teahouse streets carry you south-west to the Kamo River, where the walk ends at dusk on the bridge. Expect roughly 3.4 km of walking — about 50 minutes on the move — spread across a half day once you add the temples.

Practicalities: Kiyomizu-dera opens at 6:00 and most other sites close by 17:00, so start in the morning — in late January the sun sets about 17:30, timing the river finish exactly, and the first plum blossom is usually showing. Expect cold, near freezing on the hillside, and possible snow: bring a coat and shoes you can slip off, because several halls are entered shoeless, and carry cash — temple ticket windows often take nothing else. Admission totals roughly ¥1,100, and Kiyomizu-dera's Jishu Shrine is closed for a multi-year restoration, so check before counting on it.

So: boots on, eyes up, and let the hill do the work.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. The walk is a descent from the temple hillside, but the preserved slopes between Kiyomizu-dera and Kodai-ji are steep stone steps that get wet in winter, and Kiyomizu-dera's own grounds have long flights of steps. Nene-no-Michi, Yasaka Shrine and central Gion are level; Gion's side lanes are not.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start at Kiyomizu-dera early — it opens at 6:00, and the lanes outside are quiet until about 9:00. Work downhill through the morning, give Kodai-ji and Yasaka Shrine the early afternoon, and reach Hanamikoji in the late afternoon. In late January and early February the sun sets around 17:30, which times the finish on the Kamo River exactly. If you can only manage one early start, spend it on Kiyomizu-dera; the midday crowd there is the worst on the walk.

stops.name: Kiyomizu-dera
stops.narration:
You are standing on what Japanese calls a butai — a stage — and the phrase you are looking for is real: this wooden platform hangs about thirteen metres above the hillside, the height of a four-storey building, and there is not a single nail in it.

Look at the joinery under the rail rather than at the view. Beams run through the pillars and lock into them like furniture, not scaffolding — an old technique called kakezukuri, "hanging construction". The stage and the hall behind it were rebuilt in 1633, four years after a fire, paid for by Tokugawa Iemitsu, the third shogun, the military ruler of Japan. The whole assembly rests on the slope and rides out earthquakes by shifting.

Kiyomizu means "pure water", and the name comes from the waterfall below you, Otowa no taki, where three channels fall into a pond. Drink from one — one for long life, one for success in study, one for love — but not all three; wanting everything is considered greedy. The temple is older than the city: legend dates its founding to 778, sixteen years before Kyoto became the capital in 794, when a monk named Enchin came up this mountain following a dream.

Two practical things before you move on. Jishu Shrine, behind the main hall, is famous for two "love stones" set a few metres apart — find your way between them with your eyes closed and love will find you — but its buildings have been shut for restoration since 2022 and the work runs for years, so do not build the visit around it; check at the gate. And admission is around ¥500 for adults, ¥200 for schoolchildren, with cash the safest bet. The temple opens at 6:00 and closes about 18:00 through the winter, so come early — by ten the lane outside is a queue.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around ¥500 for adults, ¥200 for elementary and junior-high students, at the gate on the day. Cash is safest — do not assume card works at temple ticket windows. Prices change, so verify at the gate.
stops.openingHours: Opens 6:00 daily. Closing is seasonal: about 18:00 from 1 January to 26 March, later in the spring, summer and autumn night-viewing periods. Verify at the gate.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free, honestly. The approach up Kiyomizu-zaka is a slope of steps and uneven stone, and the main hall, stage and inner circuit involve further stairs. The stage is level once you are standing on it. Wheelchair routes exist but are limited; ask at the gate.
stops.insiderTip: Walk across the valley to Okuno-in, the small hall above the waterfall — the view back at the main hall and its stage from there is the photograph most people miss. On the way, stop under the stage and look up at the joinery instead of the scenery.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave through the Niō-mon gate and walk downhill with the crowd along Kiyomizu-zaka, the shopping lane, for five to ten minutes. Where the street bends, take Sannen-zaka, the stone slope dropping away on your right, and follow it down past the shops. Those slopes are the next stop; the cobbles are uneven and often wet in winter, so take the steps slowly.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sannenzaka & Ninenzaka
stops.narration:
These two lanes are not a shopping street with history attached; they are a neighbourhood that was protected just in time. Sannen-zaka, "three-year slope", and Ninen-zaka, "two-year slope", run down from Kiyomizu-dera toward the Kodai-ji quarter, and the names are a warning rather than a measurement: legend says anyone who falls on these stones will die within two or three years. Take the steps sideways when they are wet.

The real number is 1976, when the city designated this area an Important Preservation District for Groups of Traditional Buildings — among the earliest in Japan. That is why there are no power lines overhead and no cars, and why the facades in front of you are timber machiya: narrow townhouses where a family once lived behind the shop. Modern businesses occupy them now, but the proportions are the old ones — low doors, deep eaves, latticed windows.

That protection created the argument you are standing in the middle of. On a busy afternoon these lanes carry more visitors than residents, and the people who campaigned to save this streetscape are the same people now spending their mornings navigating tour groups. Kyoto's guidance to visitors is blunt: do not block a doorway to take a photograph, do not eat while walking where someone is sweeping, do not photograph into windows. It is a public street, but it is also a front garden.

Look up as you go down. The five-storey pagoda rising over the rooftops ahead is the next stop, and it is the reason these lanes exist: pilgrims have been walking this route to it and on to Kiyomizu-dera for centuries.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public streets. Shops and cafés charge their own prices, and there is no ticket for walking the slopes.
stops.openingHours: Open streets, accessible at any hour. Shops generally open around 10:00 and close between 17:00 and 18:00; the lanes are quietest before 9:00.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free. Both slopes are long flights of stone steps, often wet, with no level alternative between them. Handrails are limited. The lanes are narrow and can be shoulder-to-shoulder in peak season.
stops.insiderTip: Come before 9:00 and the same street belongs to delivery vans, shopkeepers and schoolchildren. The light is better, the photographs are of buildings rather than backs, and the residents get their street back for an hour.
stops.nextStopDirections: At the bottom of the slopes, turn right and keep walking downhill on Yasaka-dōri for two or three minutes. The tall wooden pagoda ahead on your right, rising above the rooftops, is Hōkan-ji, the Yasaka Pagoda. Stop on the pavement opposite it; the street carries traffic.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Andrea Schaffer from Sydney, Australia, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yasaka Pagoda (Hōkan-ji)
stops.narration:
That is the Yasaka Pagoda — Yasaka no Tō in Japanese — and it is the surviving building of a temple called Hōkan-ji, founded on this spot in the seventh century, which makes it one of the oldest sacred sites in the city. The tower itself is younger: what you see was rebuilt in 1440, after fire. It is the oldest five-storey pagoda in Kyoto, and without question the most photographed piece of Higashiyama.

Its history explains how much of old Kyoto was lost, and why. In 1179 this pagoda burned down in a straightforward fight over ownership: Gion Shrine, the Shinto shrine down the hill, and Kiyomizu-dera, the Buddhist temple up the hill, both claimed it, and the dispute turned to arson. In 1240 a priest from Kennin-ji, the Zen temple a few minutes west of here, brought the site under Zen Buddhism, which is still its official affiliation. Watch a shrine and a temple fight over one building and then settle into sharing it — that is Japanese religious history in miniature.

Walk a few steps up Yasaka-dōri for the classic view, with the pagoda framed at the end of the lane. But watch the traffic. This is a working street with cars and delivery vans, not a pedestrian zone, and people live along it.

The interior opens only on rare occasions, so the outside is the exhibit — and there is a lesson in that silhouette. Five roofs, stacked and shrinking, each with deep eaves that throw rain clear of the timber below. The eaves are not decoration; they are weatherproofing, the same idea you saw holding up the stage at Kiyomizu, repeated upwards.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to view from the street. The pagoda interior is usually closed and opens only on special occasions; there is no regular ticket desk.
stops.openingHours: Exterior visible at any hour. The temple interior opens only occasionally — treat the outside as the visit. The lane is a working road with traffic at all times.
stops.accessibility: Viewed from level pavement with kerbs; the temple compound itself is not generally open. The lane has traffic and narrow sections, so take care with the kerb.
stops.insiderTip: The view everyone wants is up Yasaka-dōri, a few metres downhill, with the pagoda closing the lane — but stand on the pavement, never in the roadway, for it. Early morning gives you the lane almost empty and the pagoda lit from the east.
stops.nextStopDirections: From the pagoda, follow Yasaka-dōri north-west for about two hundred metres to the junction, then turn left onto Nene-no-Michi, the flagstone lane signposted for Kodai-ji. Follow it past the shops for roughly four hundred metres. Kōdai-ji's stone staircase and gate are on your left at the top of the rise.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Kodai-ji
stops.narration:
This quiet temple is a widow's monument, and to feel its weight you need one family's story. In the late sixteenth century Japan was climbing out of the Sengoku period — the "Warring States", a century in which regional lords tore the country apart. Three men ended it. The second, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, was born a farmer's son and rose to rule all of Japan; he died in 1598 before he could finish the job. His wife, Nene, was a political partner as well as a spouse. When he died she took Buddhist vows, changed her name to Kōdai-in and, in 1606, founded this temple to pray for his soul. She lived on this site until 1624, which is why the flagstone lane you just walked is called Nene-no-Michi — Nene's path.

Hideyoshi's generation spent war money on gold screens and tea rooms, and a Zen temple like this is where you see what that bought. The gardens are dry-landscape gardens — karesansui, where raked gravel and borrowed scenery stand in for water and mountains — traditionally credited to Kobori Enshū, the tea master and garden designer of the age. Two of them face each other across the main hall. Walk slowly; the moss, the gravel and the rooflines of the city below do the work.

There is a hard political fact underneath the beauty. After Hideyoshi died, the rival Tokugawa family took power and hunted his heir. Nene's decision to become a nun and build a Zen temple, rather than a political tomb, is part of why she and this place survived.

Admission is around ¥600 for adults, sometimes quoted higher when the on-site Sho Museum is bundled in, so check at the gate — prices move. Hours are roughly 9:00 to 17:30 with last entry at 17:00, and the paths are gravel and moss, so dry-weather shoes are kinder to you.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Around ¥600 for adults, ¥250 for junior-high and high-school students, usually including the on-site Sho Museum; some sources quote a higher bundled ticket, so verify at the gate. A combined ticket with neighbouring Entoku-in is also sold.
stops.openingHours: Roughly 9:00 to 17:30, last entry 17:00. Seasonal night illuminations, when held, run much later into the evening — check dates at the gate or online.
stops.accessibility: Partly stepped. The approach is a stone staircase, and inside the grounds the paths are gravel and moss with some steps between the halls and gardens. Not step-free; a wheelchair route is limited.
stops.insiderTip: The bamboo grove behind the main hall is often empty even when the gardens are busy, and the two facing dry gardens read best from the corner where the raked gravel and the borrowed skyline line up. That corner is where the garden's argument makes sense.
stops.nextStopDirections: Come back down Nene-no-Michi and continue north for about six hundred metres, following the signs and the flow of people toward Gion. Yasaka Shrine's stone torii and its red gate rise at the end of the street — walk under the gate into the grounds. It is roughly ten minutes, mostly level.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Qwert1234, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Yasaka Shrine
stops.narration:
You are at a shrine more than 1,350 years old — founded, by tradition, in 656, long before Kyoto was a capital at all. This is Shinto, Japan's older religion: a faith of places, built around kami, sacred presences tied to nature, ancestors and legend, and around purification. A torii gate marks where ordinary ground ends. The kami enshrined here is Susanoo-no-Mikoto, the storm-and-sea god of Japan's oldest myths.

Look at the main hall behind the vermilion gate. It was rebuilt in 1654 on the orders of Tokugawa Ietsuna, the fourth shogun — the military ruler — and in 2020 Japan designated it a National Treasure, the highest protection the country gives a building. Its style, Gion-zukuri, wraps a deep roof right around the veranda.

This is also the home of Japan's most famous festival. In 869 a plague was killing people in the city and the emperor ordered prayers here; sixty-six halberds, one for each province of Japan, were carried in procession to appease the spirits behind the disease. That ritual grew into the Gion Matsuri, held every July for more than a thousand years — enormous wheeled floats through the streets on 17 and 24 July, and a portable shrine, a mikoshi, carried on men's shoulders.

Note the name change. For most of its life this was Gion Shrine, tangled up with Buddhist temples. In 1868 the reforming Meiji government ordered Shinto and Buddhism separated by law, and the shrine was renamed Yasaka. That was politics, not theology, and you can still see its seams all over Kyoto.

The grounds are free and open around the clock; the office for amulets and stamps keeps roughly 9:00 to 17:00, and the lanterns are lit in the evening. If you are here on 2 or 3 February, come back — maiko and geiko dance at Setsubun and throw roasted beans to the crowd.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter. Amulets, charms and the calligraphic goshuin stamp are sold separately at the shrine office; nothing is required.
stops.openingHours: Grounds open 24 hours, free. The amulet, charm and goshuin office keeps roughly 9:00 to 17:00. Lanterns are lit in the evening.
stops.accessibility: Mostly level gravel and stone paths through the grounds, with a few steps at the inner halls and at the western exits. The main approach from Shijō-dōri is flat and step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Come back after dark: the shrine is free and open all night, the lanterns are lit, and the crimson gate against a dark sky is the shot. Also find Utsukushi-gozen-sha, the small sub-shrine for beauty just inside the grounds, where geiko and maiko come to pray.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave Yasaka Shrine by its western gate and walk downhill past the shrine buildings to Shijō-dōri. At the traffic lights turn left, catch the big gate on the far side, and cross onto Hanamikoji. That street running south between the teahouses is the next stop — about ten minutes from the shrine.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: DXR, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Gion & Hanamikoji Street
stops.narration:
You are on Hanamikoji, the main street of Gion, and this district is a workplace, not a stage set. Gion is one of Kyoto's five hanamachi — "flower towns", the quarters where geiko and maiko live and train. Geiko is the Kyoto word for geisha: a professional entertainer, not a courtesan, who trains for years in dance, in the shamisen, a three-stringed lute, in tea and in conversation, and who performs at private banquets. A maiko is an apprentice, usually still a teenager, recognisable by the long obi sash hanging at her back and the red collar. Kyoto has roughly two hundred geiko and maiko across its five districts; in the early 1900s they numbered in the tens of thousands nationwide.

Three institutions run the system. An okiya is the lodging house where maiko live and train. An ochaya is the teahouse where the banquets actually happen — the wooden houses with slatted lattice fronts, built so that guests inside can look out and the street cannot look in. And by tradition an ochaya refuses first-time customers without an introduction from an existing regular; the principle is ichigensan okotowari, "no first-time visitors". That is not snobbery to argue with. It is how a small, expensive, referral-run world protects itself.

So here is the rule, and it is hard: do not stop, follow, touch or photograph geiko or maiko unless they invite it. Photography is banned outright in the private side lanes, with a ¥10,000 fine, and residents pushed for that enforcement. Hanamikoji itself is a public road with cars — do not block it.

If you want to see the arts performed, buy a ticket. Gion Corner at the Kaburenjo theatre stages an hour of tea ceremony, koto music, flower arrangement and Kyomai dance by maiko, usually at 18:00 and 19:00, around ¥5,500 for adults; in April the same theatre hosts the Miyako Odori. That is the respectful way in.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to walk the public street. Performances are ticketed separately — Gion Corner is around ¥5,500 for adults; verify current prices and showtimes.
stops.openingHours: Public street, accessible at any hour, though the district quiets after dark. Teahouses and restaurants are private and not open to visitors. Gion Corner's shows usually run at 18:00 and 19:00; its winter programme runs Tuesday to Friday and it closes over the New Year.
stops.accessibility: Level paved street with kerbs, busy with cars and pedestrians. The private side lanes off Hanamikoji are narrow and some have steps; several are now off-limits to visitors.
stops.insiderTip: The guaranteed, respectful way to see geiko and maiko perform is to buy a ticket for Gion Corner, the hour-long show at the Kaburenjo just south of here, or the Miyako Odori in April. Do not stake out the lanes hoping for a passing maiko.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk Hanamikoji to its northern end at Shijō-dōri, turn right, and cross at the lights; within a minute the buildings open and you are on the bridge over the Kamo River. Go down the stone steps on the left to the riverbank. About seven hundred metres in total.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: The Kamo River at Shijō
stops.narration:
End on the riverbank, because everything you just walked through exists because of where it sits. This is the Kamo River — Kamo-gawa, "duck river" — and it was the eastern edge of the ancient city. In 794 the emperor Kanmu moved Japan's capital here and named it Heian-kyō, "capital of peace and tranquillity". He copied the plan of Chang'an, the Tang dynasty capital in China: a rectangle with a great north–south avenue down the middle and a grid of numbered streets. You have been walking inside that grid all day. Shijō, under your feet, simply means "fourth avenue".

The river did the job a city wall does elsewhere. Beyond it rose the hills, and onto those hills the temples crowded — the ones you have spent the day in. The Kamo is shallow, usually less than a metre deep and useless for boats, which is part of why Kyoto never became a port. Instead it became the city's open-air living room: people walk the banks, jog, sit on the stone steps and watch the herons. In summer, restaurants across the water build wooden terraces called noryo-yuka right out over the shallows. In January those are gone and the river runs cold and fast, which is its own pleasure.

Across the water is Pontocho, a single narrow lane of restaurants and one of Kyoto's other geisha districts; its geiko and maiko perform the Kamogawa Odori here every May.

You are finishing at dusk, on purpose. The lanterns come on along the bridge, the hills go blue, and the day stacks up behind you: a stage, two slopes, a pagoda fought over by a shrine and a temple, a widow's Zen garden, and the latticed fronts of the teahouses. All of it built by people who looked at this river while they did it.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free riverside promenade and bridge. Restaurants, cafés and the Pontocho lanes charge their own prices; nothing here requires a ticket.
stops.openingHours: Open at any hour, free. The riverside is unlit at night away from the bridges — best at dusk and into the early evening.
stops.accessibility: The bridge is level with pavements on both sides, and the upper promenade along the bank is step-free. The stone steps down to the water's edge are steep and uneven, and the lower path can flood after rain.
stops.insiderTip: Walk a few minutes south along the bank toward Gojō for the same view without the bridge crowd, then look back north at the lit windows of Pontocho. In winter the herons stand in the shallows; in summer the noryo-yuka terraces hang over the water here.
stops.nextStopDirections: That is the end of the walk. If you are hungry, Pontocho's narrow lane of restaurants begins just north across the road; the covered shopping streets of Kawaramachi and Teramachi are a few minutes west for coffee or a bookshop. Gion-Shijō station on the Keihan line is two minutes east along Shijō, and Kyoto Station is a short train ride south. Winter sunset comes early here, so if you want to see the river lit, plan to arrive before dark rather than after it.
